nodes.title: The ARC
nodes.summary: ZFS's adaptive read cache—the reason your RAM looks full, and why that's the system working, not leaking.

nodes.title: Ashift
nodes.summary: The sector-size assumption baked into a vdev at creation—immutable forever, and the one setting a wrong guess makes permanent. Use 12.

nodes.title: Checksums
nodes.summary: Every block verified on every read, with the checksum stored apart from the data—detection is unconditional; repair needs a second good copy.

nodes.title: Compression
nodes.summary: LZ4 is so fast the old space-vs-CPU trade runs backward—compression on is the default posture, and it often makes the pool faster.

nodes.title: Copy-on-Write
nodes.summary: ZFS never overwrites a live block—every write lands on fresh space and pointers flip atomically. Not a safety feature; the ontology everything else stands on.
entry_points: why does zfs not need fsck

nodes.title: Datasets
nodes.summary: Not folders and not partitions—nearly-free policy boundaries carved from the pool's shared space. The unit of properties, snapshots, and replication. Make many.
entry_points: how many datasets should i make

nodes.title: Deduplication
nodes.summary: Sounds free because checksums already exist—actually a standing RAM tax on every write, forever, that loses to plain compression in almost every homelab.

nodes.title: The ECC Question
nodes.summary: "ZFS without ECC eats your data" is the loudest myth in homelab ZFS—the scrub-of-death mechanism doesn't survive inspection, per the co-creator himself.
entry_points: do i need ecc ram for zfs

nodes.title: A Short History of Filesystems
nodes.summary: Fifty years in one story: each generation of filesystems answers the previous generation's disaster—ending (so far) at the generation ZFS opened, which stopped trusting the disk itself.
entry_points: why are there so many filesystems

nodes.title: The Filesystem Landscape
nodes.summary: The filesystems you actually meet—ext4, XFS, NTFS, APFS, Btrfs—one honest line each, and the specific combination ZFS offers that the others don't.

nodes.title: Your First Pool
nodes.summary: The creation decisions in the order they lock in: vdev shape and ashift are forever, everything else is a property. One command, four judgments.

nodes.title: The Free-Space Discipline
nodes.summary: On a CoW pool, free space isn't headroom—it's the workshop floor every write operates on. Fill the pool and the pool gets permanently grumpier.
entry_points: how full can a zfs pool get

nodes.title: L2ARC
nodes.summary: The ARC's spillover tier on SSD—every block it caches costs ARC RAM for the index, so it's a measured fix for proven ARC misses, not free speed.
entry_points: should i add a cache drive

nodes.title: Mirrors
nodes.summary: Two-plus disks holding identical copies—half your capacity for the best IOPS, the fastest resilvers, and the most flexible growth. The workhorse layout for VM and database pools.

nodes.title: Mountpoints
nodes.summary: ZFS mounts itself—the mountpoint is a property of the dataset, stored in the pool, traveling with the data. fstab isn't empty by accident.

nodes.title: The Pool
nodes.summary: One shared reservoir of storage built from vdevs—not a big partition, and not where redundancy lives.

nodes.title: Import and Export
nodes.summary: The pool's entire self-description lives on its member disks—any machine with OpenZFS can import them and get everything, mounts included. Data was never married to the machine.
entry_points: motherboard died is my data safe

nodes.title: Property Inheritance
nodes.summary: Properties set on a dataset flow down its subtree until overridden—policy is written once at the right altitude, not per-dataset.

nodes.title: ZFS Under Proxmox
nodes.summary: What the installer actually built: an rpool for the OS, zvols per VM disk, and an ARC that shares RAM with your VMs—the homelab's most common ZFS, decoded.

nodes.title: RAIDZ
nodes.summary: Parity redundancy that fixed RAID5's write hole—but a RAIDZ vdev delivers roughly one disk of IOPS no matter how wide. Bulk storage, not VM storage.

nodes.title: RAIDZ Expansion
nodes.summary: Since OpenZFS 2.3 you can widen a RAIDZ vdev live—with caveats: old data keeps its old parity ratio, and type still can't change.
entry_points: can i add a disk to raidz

nodes.title: Recordsize
nodes.summary: Not the disk's block size—the maximum logical block per file, set per dataset. It matters when small random I/O lands inside big files, and it only touches new files.

nodes.title: Replacing a Disk
nodes.summary: The procedure you'll run under stress, made boring: identify by serial, replace, watch the resilver, scrub. The real risk is precision, not speed.
entry_points: disk died what do i do
how to replace a failed disk

nodes.title: Resilvering
nodes.summary: ZFS's rebuild—but it copies live data, not disk sectors, verifying every block against its checksum. Emptier pool, shorter rebuild, smaller second-failure window.

nodes.title: Rollback
nodes.summary: Not timeline navigation—demolition. Rolling back to Tuesday destroys everything after Tuesday, permanently. Clones and .zfs/snapshot are the gentle paths.

nodes.title: Sanoid and Syncoid
nodes.summary: Not a backup daemon—two thin tools: sanoid is policy over snapshot/destroy, syncoid is orchestration over send/recv. Judgment on top of primitives you can run by hand.

nodes.title: Scrubs
nodes.summary: A forced read of everything, so checksums can catch silent damage while redundancy still exists to repair it. Detection is unconditional; repair isn't.

nodes.title: Send and Receive
nodes.summary: Not rsync with extra steps—a serialized exact snapshot state, with incrementals diffed by block birth-time. rsync approximates sameness; recv is sameness.
entry_points: how to copy a dataset to another machine

nodes.title: Snapshots
nodes.summary: A snapshot copies nothing—it's a named pin on blocks that already exist. Free at creation; the cost arrives later, as the present diverges from the pinned past.

nodes.title: Snapshots and Disappearing Space
nodes.summary: You deleted the files and the space didn't come back—because snapshots still reference them. The space moved ledgers; it didn't free.
entry_points: deleted files but no space freed

nodes.title: Snapshots Are Not Backups
nodes.summary: A snapshot lives on the same disks, in the same pool, behind the same mistakes as the data. It's the versioning half of a backup strategy; replication is the other half.
entry_points: do i need backups with zfs

nodes.title: The Vdev
nodes.summary: The unit of redundancy—and therefore the unit of failure. The pool survives any disk its vdevs can absorb, and dies with any vdev it can't.

nodes.title: What a Filesystem Is
nodes.summary: The absolute ground floor: a disk stores only numbered blocks and has no idea what a file is—the filesystem is the ledger that invents files, names, and folders on top of them.

nodes.title: What ZFS Is
nodes.summary: Not a filesystem with features—the whole storage stack rebuilt around one act of distrust: assume the hardware lies, verify everything, never depend on an overwrite.

nodes.title: ZIL and SLOG
nodes.summary: Not a write cache—a crash-recovery log that's written constantly and read exactly once, after a crash. A SLOG only moves it to faster media, and only synchronous writes care.

nodes.title: Reading zpool status
nodes.summary: The pool's one health report—and DEGRADED means the design is working, not that the pool is dying. How to read it without panic.

nodes.title: Zvols
nodes.summary: A dataset wearing a block-device face—pool-backed raw volumes with snapshots and send/recv, no filesystem-in-a-file. What Proxmox gives VMs.
